summaries.gardner: Procter & Gamble is a classic 'Rule Maker' rather than a Rule Breaker: it is the top dog in mature household and personal care markets, with organic sales up only 1% in fiscal 2026. It has a famous brand portfolio and a strong management bench, but it lacks the emerging-industry leadership, momentum (a 6.7% one-year total return vs about 17% for the S&P 500) and 'overvalued' label Gardner looks for.
summaries.buffett: P&G has many Buffett traits: a simple business, trusted brands such as Tide, Pampers and Gillette, 70 straight years of dividend increases and a return on invested capital of about 21.5%. Berkshire Hathaway exchanged its P&G stake for Duracell in 2016, and at about 23 times trailing earnings with low single-digit growth there is little margin of safety today.
summaries.munger: Thinking backwards, there are few ways for P&G to fail: its brands, scale and retail relationships make sudden collapse unlikely. Munger would likely see a high-quality but slow-growing business at a full price, with private label, commodity costs and retailer power as the main forces to watch.
summaries.lynch: P&G is Lynch's textbook stalwart: a giant, steady company with a simple story of selling everyday products a little better and at slightly higher prices each year. Its trailing P/E of about 23 is far above its earnings growth (diluted EPS up 2% in fiscal 2026, core EPS guided flat to up 3% for fiscal 2027), and the stock is anything but overlooked.
summaries.fisher: P&G scores well on Fisher's points about sales and marketing skill, steady product renewal (for example Tide and Dawn reformulations), management depth and long-term outlook. It is weaker on his growth and margin points, since gross margin slipped from 51.2% in fiscal 2025 to 50.2% in fiscal 2026 and volume was flat.
summaries.graham: P&G passes Graham's tests for size, a dividend paid every year since 1890, profits in every one of the last ten years and EPS growth (diluted EPS from continuing operations rose from $3.49 in fiscal 2016 to $6.62 in fiscal 2026). It fails the valuation tests: about 24 times three-year average earnings and P/E times P/B of about 154, against Graham's limits of 15 and 22.5.
summaries.thiel: P&G has a durable position and a distribution machine few can match, which fits Thiel's questions on durability and distribution. It has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals, no hidden secret and no fresh market to dominate, so it scores poorly on most of his seven questions.
summaries.gerstner: P&G is not the kind of high-growth, technology-led company Gerstner usually backs, with fiscal 2027 sales growth guided at 1% to 3%. Its cost discipline and restructuring fit his 'get fit' theme, but about 22 times forward earnings is a full price for that growth.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings, rising estimates and macro tailwinds; P&G has none of these, with core EPS guided flat to up 3% for fiscal 2027, a roughly $1 billion after-tax commodity headwind, and a share price that trailed the market over the past year. It is a defensive holding rather than a high-conviction bet.
summaries.smith: P&G fits Terry Smith's 'good company' test well: a gross margin of about 50%, ROIC of about 21.5%, resilient repeat-purchase demand and adjusted free cash flow equal to 100% of earnings in fiscal 2026, and Fundsmith has owned consumer staples like it. The question is the 'don't overpay' rule at about 24 times free cash flow (a 4.2% free-cash-flow yield) for low single-digit growth.
summaries.greenblatt: P&G has a high return on capital (ROIC about 21.5%) but a modest earnings yield: GAAP operating income of $19,748M against an enterprise value of about $387B is about 5.1%. It would rank only mid-pack on a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: P&G is strong on Akre's first leg (an extraordinary business with high returns) and solid on management, but weak on the reinvestment leg: in fiscal 2026 it returned $10,232M in dividends and $5,028M in buybacks, close to all of its $16,046M of net earnings, because it cannot reinvest much at high returns.
summaries.pabrai: P&G offers a very low risk of permanent loss, but there is no Dhandho-style distress or deep discount: the shares trade at about 23 times earnings and Nash-style cash-flow math at a 12% discount rate values them far below the price. Pabrai's 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' at a low price is not present.
summaries.wood: P&G is not involved in any of ARK's innovation platforms (AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing), and its markets grow slowly. It does not fit Cathie Wood's approach.
summaries.ackman: P&G matches many Pershing Square criteria: simple, predictable, free-cash-flow generative, with high barriers to entry from brands and scale. Ackman would likely want a larger discount to intrinsic value than about 22 times forward earnings, and P&G is exposed to commodity costs and currencies, which he prefers to avoid.
summaries.sleep: P&G has the durable brands and scale Nick Sleep valued, but it uses its scale mainly to defend margins and raise prices rather than to pass savings to customers in a 'scale economies shared' way. Its position in 10-20 years looks secure but not clearly stronger than today, given private-label pressure.
summaries.valentine: P&G is a company founded in 1837 selling into mature markets, not a fast-growing new market created by technology. It sits outside Don Valentine's venture approach.
summaries.nash: P&G fails most of Nash's hard filters: revenue grew only 3.3% in fiscal 2026, total debt of $34,138M is far above cash of $9,942M, operating expenses grew faster than sales and it rides no secular trend. It scores well on moat, pricing power, earnings beats and low short interest, but totals about 65 on the scorecard and a Nash-style DCF at 12% gives about $67 a share against roughly $156.

momentum.evidence: PG's total return over the year to Oct 13, 2026 was 6.68% (price about $155.78), well behind the S&P 500's 17.34% over the same period.

g4.evidence: P&G has a renowned promote-from-within management bench (CEO Shailesh Jejurikar since January 2026, executive chairman Jon Moeller) and 71% institutional ownership, but no celebrated investor backs it; Berkshire Hathaway swapped its P&G shares for Duracell in 2016.

g6.evidence: Analysts are mostly positive (25 analysts with a consensus Buy and an average target of about $161, StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), and at about 22 times forward earnings it is not widely called overvalued.

simple.evidence: It makes and sells everyday branded products like Tide, Pampers, Charmin, Crest and Gillette through retailers, a business any careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Net sales rose every year from $76,118M in fiscal 2021 to $87,032M in fiscal 2026, and the dividend has been raised for 70 consecutive years.

integrity.evidence: Management gives clear guidance with full non-GAAP reconciliations, returned $15,260M through dividends and buybacks in fiscal 2026, and handed over from Jon Moeller to Shailesh Jejurikar in an orderly, pre-announced succession.

b6.evidence: P&G has shrunk rather than empire-built, divesting around 100 brands in 2014-2017 and exiting some categories and markets in its 2025 restructuring.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 21.5% and ROE about 30% (StockAnalysis), with moderate debt of 0.64 times equity and interest covered about 22.5 times by fiscal 2026 operating income.

fcf.evidence: Fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of $19,556M less capital spending of $4,409M gave free cash flow of $15,147M, and P&G reported adjusted free-cash-flow productivity of 100%.

b10.evidence: P&G pays out nearly all its earnings (fiscal 2026 dividends $10,232M plus buybacks $5,028M vs net earnings $16,046M), so little is retained, and its 10-year total return of 112.47% to Oct 2026 is respectable but not exceptional.

safety.evidence: At about $155.78 the shares trade at about 23 times trailing EPS and 6.7 times book, and a Nash-style DCF at 12% gives about $67 a share, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 22 is high for core EPS guided at $6.89-$7.11 for fiscal 2027 (flat to up 3%), with a PEG of about 4.4, though a premium is usual for its quality and stability.

mu5.evidence: With leading brands in about 180 countries across ten categories, the main failure paths are slow erosion from private label and retailer power, not collapse.

reinvest.evidence: Capital spending of $4,409M in fiscal 2026 was far below the $15,260M returned to shareholders, because slow-growing categories offer few large high-return reinvestment opportunities.

ly2.evidence: P&G is a classic stalwart: low single-digit organic sales growth, about 50% gross margins and 70 years of rising dividends.

ly3.evidence: Its trailing P/E of about 23 is far above its earnings growth rate (diluted EPS up 2% in fiscal 2026 and guided up 1% to 5% for fiscal 2027).

runway.evidence: Management guides fiscal 2027 sales growth of only 1% to 3%, and volume was flat in fiscal 2026, so there is no long runway of substantial growth.

ly7.evidence: No open-market insider purchases show in recent Form 4 filings (mainly director stock grants), but buybacks cut weighted diluted shares from 2,601M in fiscal 2021 to 2,422.5M in fiscal 2026.

ly8.evidence: P&G is one of the most widely owned and covered stocks in the world, with about 71% institutional ownership and 25 covering analysts.

fi2.evidence: P&G steadily renews its products with upgrades such as new Tide and Dawn formulas, Oral-B iO electric toothbrushes and Swiffer line extensions as older versions mature.

fi3.evidence: Its research has kept brands like Tide, Gillette and Oral-B ahead on performance, but recent innovation has not been enough to lift volume, which was flat in fiscal 2026.

fi4.evidence: P&G is one of the world's largest advertisers and is famed for brand-building and retail execution, holding over 60% of blades and razors and about 30% of global oral and baby care.

longterm.evidence: Management keeps investing in brand superiority and supply-chain upgrades, accepting restructuring charges of $749M in fiscal 2026 to strengthen the business over the long term.

gr1.evidence: P&G had $87,032M of fiscal 2026 sales and a market value of about $362B.

ni10.evidence: P&G has been profitable in each of the last ten fiscal years, with net earnings attributable to P&G of $16,046M in fiscal 2026.

gr4.evidence: P&G has paid a dividend every year since 1890 and has raised it for 70 consecutive years.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS from continuing operations rose from $3.49 in fiscal 2016 to $6.62 in fiscal 2026, an increase of about 90%.

gr6.evidence: At about $155.78 the price is about 24 times the fiscal 2024-2026 average diluted EPS of $6.38.

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 23.1 times a P/B of about 6.67 gives about 154, far above Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: P&G's advantage is brands, scale and know-how, not a technology ten times better than rivals; store brands often match performance at lower prices.

timing.evidence: Demand for household staples is steady, but cost-conscious shoppers trading down, tariffs and commodity costs make the current timing unfavourable for growth.

th3.evidence: P&G began as a small Cincinnati soap and candle maker in 1837 and expanded category by category, but today it competes in huge, mature markets with no new small market to dominate.

team.evidence: Its management is experienced and well regarded (Jejurikar was COO from 2021 as sales grew from $76.1B to $87.0B), but it is a strong professional team rather than an exceptional founder-led one.

th5.evidence: P&G sells through every major retailer, including Walmart (about 16% of sales), with priority shelf space and advertising scale few rivals can match.

durable.evidence: P&G has led household and personal care for decades and its brands and retail relationships make its position very likely to hold for 10-20 years, though private label will keep chipping at it.

th7.evidence: Its opportunity is well understood by everyone; there is no hidden secret.

trend.evidence: P&G is not a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift such as AI or cloud computing.

dr1.evidence: Earnings are decelerating: Q4 fiscal 2026 diluted EPS fell 15% and core EPS 3%, and consensus sees fiscal 2027 core EPS up only about 1.3% to $6.98.

dr2.evidence: Savings from the 2025 restructuring could lift margins by fiscal 2028, but a roughly $1 billion after-tax commodity headwind and flat volume weigh on the next 18-24 months.

dr4.evidence: As a defensive staple with a beta of 0.38 it holds up in slowdowns, but higher rates make its 2.8% dividend yield less attractive and tariffs and commodity costs hurt margins.

dr6.evidence: Restructuring savings, product launches and Q1 fiscal 2027 results due around October 22, 2026 are identifiable events, but none is likely to change growth sharply.

dr7.evidence: With growth guided at 1% to 3% and estimates barely rising, conviction is not high enough for a large concentrated position in Druckenmiller's sense.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 50.2% in fiscal 2026, high for consumer goods, though down from 51.2% in fiscal 2025.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 4.2% (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), reasonable for a stable staple but not cheap for low single-digit growth.

gb2.evidence: GAAP operating income of $19,748M against an enterprise value of about $387B is an operating earnings yield of only about 5.1%.

pa2.evidence: Flat volume, commodity and tariff costs and restructuring charges in fiscal 2026 look like fixable pressures, but the stock is not deeply depressed and slow growth may be structural.

pa4.evidence: With dominant brands, a beta of 0.38, 70 years of dividend increases and interest coverage above 20 times, the chance of permanent loss of the business is small, though overpaying is a risk.

wo1.evidence: P&G is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Its product costs do not fall quickly with volume; P&G expects higher commodity costs and has raised prices instead.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Household and personal care grows roughly with population and incomes, so its market cannot become many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Demand is steady, but P&G is exposed to commodity costs (about a $1 billion after-tax headwind expected in fiscal 2027), tariffs and currency swings from selling in about 180 countries.

ns1.evidence: P&G uses its scale mainly to defend margins and raise prices rather than to cut prices for customers, which leaves room for cheaper private label.

ns4.evidence: Its brands should remain leaders in 10-20 years, but private label, e-commerce and local rivals make a clearly stronger position unlikely.

va2.evidence: Its products meet universal everyday needs such as hygiene, cleaning and baby care, but these are solved problems with many good alternatives rather than large unsolved pain.

tn1.evidence: P&G sells household staples and is not built around a secular trend such as AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees P&G as a slow-growing consumer staples company, and that is what it is.

tn3.evidence: It is a $362B US large cap that is not Chinese, a commodity producer, an airline, seasonal or a startup.

tn9.evidence: It trips an instant kill: total debt of $34,138M is more than three times cash of $9,942M, and revenue growth is below 10% (guided at 1% to 3% for fiscal 2027).

tn10.evidence: P&G faces routine product-liability and tariff issues but no major regulatory or legal threat to the business.

tn11.evidence: P&G provides trusted branded household and personal care products that help families stay clean and healthy, and charges per unit sold through retailers; shoppers choose it for proven performance and trust in brands like Tide and Pampers.
